title: Nature's design office
instructions: Read the article about engineers who copy designs from nature. Choose the most suitable heading (A–J) for each paragraph (1–7). There are two extra headings that you do not need to use. There is an example (0) at the beginning.
instructionsHu: Olvasd el a természet megoldásait utánzó mérnökökről szóló cikket, és válaszd ki minden bekezdéshez (1–7) a legmegfelelőbb címet (A–J). Két cím felesleges. A 0. a példa.

passage.title: Nature's design office
passage.subtitle: Why engineers and architects are turning to plants and animals for ideas

blocks.text: In Professor Ingrid Halvorsen's office at a technical university in Copenhagen, the most valuable objects are not computers but drawers. They are full of seed heads, feathers, beetle shells and the dried wings of butterflies. 'Every one of these is the answer to an engineering problem,' she says, picking up a pine cone that opens and closes depending on the humidity. 'Evolution has been testing designs for almost four billion years. We have been doing serious engineering for a few centuries. It would be foolish not to study the results.' This approach, known as biomimicry, is now taught at design schools all over the world.

One of its earliest successes began with a nuisance. In 1941, the Swiss engineer George de Mestral came home from a walk in the mountains to find his trousers and his dog's fur covered in burrs, the prickly seed cases of a common weed. Instead of simply throwing them away, he examined one under a microscope and saw hundreds of tiny hooks that caught on anything with a loop. It took him more than ten years, and plenty of mockery from textile manufacturers, to turn the idea into a fabric that worked. Today his hook-and-loop fastener holds together everything from children's shoes to astronauts' equipment.

Half a century later, a very different problem was solved by a birdwatcher. Japan's high-speed trains had become victims of their own speed: whenever one shot out of a tunnel, it pushed a wave of compressed air ahead of it, producing a loud bang that could be heard hundreds of metres away. Residents complained, and the railway faced strict noise limits. Eiji Nakatsu, an engineer and keen amateur ornithologist, remembered how the kingfisher dives from the air into water, a much denser medium, with hardly a splash. A new front end modelled on the bird's long, narrow beak made the trains quieter and, as a bonus, reduced their electricity use.

In Harare, the capital of Zimbabwe, the architect Mick Pearce turned to an even smaller teacher. Some species of termite build enormous mounds that stay at a remarkably steady temperature, even though the air outside swings between hot days and cold nights. Pearce designed an office and shopping centre that copies what he believed was the insects' secret: a network of channels that lets warm air escape through the top and draws cooler air in from below. The building, which opened in 1996, has no conventional air conditioning and uses a fraction of the energy of similar buildings. Ironically, later studies suggested that the mounds may work rather differently from the way Pearce imagined. His building, fortunately, does not seem to mind.

Not every story has such a happy ending. At the Sydney Olympics in 2000, many medal-winning swimmers wore suits that were said to imitate the rough skin of sharks, and the shark was celebrated as the latest genius of design. When biologists tested the fabric in a laboratory years later, however, they found that its surface did almost nothing to reduce drag in the way that real sharkskin does. Whatever helped those swimmers, it was probably not the shark. Imitating what a natural surface looks like, it turns out, is not the same as understanding what it does.

The field is expanding rapidly today, largely thanks to new technology. Many of nature's cleverest tricks happen at a scale far too small for the human eye. Powerful microscopes have shown, for example, that a gecko can walk across a ceiling because of millions of microscopic hairs on its feet, and that lotus leaves stay clean because their surface is covered in tiny bumps that make water roll off, taking dirt with it. With 3D printers and computer models, engineers can now reproduce such structures instead of merely admiring them. Self-cleaning paints and reusable sticky tapes based on these discoveries are already on the market.

Halvorsen is quick to point out, however, that nature is not a perfect designer. Evolution cannot plan ahead or start again with a clean sheet; it can only make small improvements to whatever already exists. The human eye, for instance, has a blind spot because of the way its nerves are wired, a fault that no engineer would deliberately build into a camera. 'Students sometimes assume that if something is natural, it must be the best solution,' she says. 'It isn't. An animal only has to be good enough to survive. Our job is to work out which of its features are brilliant and which are simply accidents of history.'

That task is becoming more urgent. Biologists estimate that most species on Earth have not yet been described, let alone studied, and many are disappearing before anyone has had the chance to look at them closely. For Halvorsen, this is the most practical argument for protecting wildlife that she knows. 'People talk about saving nature because it is beautiful, and it is,' she says. 'But every time a species dies out, we also lose solutions that took millions of years to develop. It is like burning a library before anyone has read the books.'

options.text: Why engineers should stop copying nature
A successful copy of a misunderstood original
Losing answers before we find them
When a copy is only skin-deep
Overnight success for a simple idea
A hobby solves a noisy problem

example.explanation: E – Nature's long head start (a természet hatalmas előnye). A bekezdés lényege, hogy az evolúció majdnem négymilliárd éve „teszteli” a megoldásokat, mi pedig csak néhány évszázada mérnökösködünk – ezért érdemes a természettől tanulni.
example.evidence: Evolution has been testing designs for almost four billion years.

items.explanation: B – A souvenir nobody wanted (egy emlék, amit senki sem akart). A bekezdés a tépőzár születéséről szól: de Mestral a sétáról hazatérve bogáncstermésekkel teleragadt nadrágot és kutyát talált – ez a bosszantó, nem kívánt „szuvenír” vezetett a találmányhoz.
items.evidence: came home from a walk in the mountains to find his trousers and his dog's fur covered in burrs

wrongOptions.H: Csábító, mert egyszerű ötletről van szó, de a siker nem egyik napról a másikra jött: több mint tíz évig tartott, és a textilgyártók ki is gúnyolták („more than ten years, and plenty of mockery”).

items.explanation: I – A hobby solves a noisy problem (egy hobbi megold egy zajos problémát). A gyorsvonatok hangos durranást okoztak az alagutakból kiérve; a megoldást egy lelkes amatőr madármegfigyelő mérnök találta meg a jégmadár csőre alapján.
items.evidence: Eiji Nakatsu, an engineer and keen amateur ornithologist, remembered how the kingfisher dives from the air into water

wrongOptions.B: A B a bosszantó bogáncstermésekre (1. bekezdés) illik; itt nincs szó semmilyen nem kívánt tárgyról, hanem egy zajprobléma megoldásáról.

items.explanation: D – A successful copy of a misunderstood original (sikeres másolat egy félreértett eredetiről). Az épület jól működik, pedig a későbbi kutatások szerint a termeszvárak valószínűleg nem úgy működnek, ahogy az építész gondolta – vagyis rosszul értett mintát másolt, mégis sikerrel.
items.evidence: Ironically, later studies suggested that the mounds may work rather differently from the way Pearce imagined.

wrongOptions.G: A G sikertelen, csak felszínes utánzásról szól (cápabőrös úszódressz, 4. bekezdés); a hararei épület viszont sikeres: hagyományos légkondicionálás nélkül, az energia töredékével működik.

items.explanation: G – When a copy is only skin-deep (amikor a másolat csak felszínes). A „skin-deep” jelentése: felszínes, csak a külsőt érinti. Az úszódresszek csak kinézetre utánozták a cápabőrt, a működését nem – a bekezdés utolsó mondata pontosan ezt mondja ki.
items.evidence: Imitating what a natural surface looks like, it turns out, is not the same as understanding what it does.

wrongOptions.C: Csábító, mert kudarcról van szó, de a szöveg nem mondja, hogy fel kellene hagyni a természet utánzásával – csak azt, hogy a puszta külső másolása nem elég.

items.explanation: J – Seeing – and building – the invisible (a láthatatlan meglátása és megépítése). A terület az új technológiák miatt fejlődik: a mikroszkópok megmutatják a szabad szemmel láthatatlan szerkezeteket (gekkó lábának szőrei, lótuszlevél dudorai), a 3D-nyomtatók pedig lehetővé teszik a lemásolásukat.
items.evidence: Many of nature's cleverest tricks happen at a scale far too small for the human eye.

wrongOptions.H: Itt sem egyetlen ötlet gyors sikeréről van szó, hanem arról, hogy az új eszközök miatt az egész terület gyorsan bővül.

items.explanation: A – Not everything natural is ideal (nem minden természetes dolog tökéletes). Halvorsen szerint a természet nem tökéletes tervező: az evolúció csak a meglévőt javítgatja, ezért vannak hibák is (pl. a szem vakfoltja), és az állatnak csak „elég jónak” kell lennie a túléléshez.
items.evidence: Halvorsen is quick to point out, however, that nature is not a perfect designer.

wrongOptions.C: Csábító, mert a természet hibáiról van szó, de Halvorsen nem azt mondja, hogy ne másoljuk, hanem hogy válogassuk ki, mely tulajdonságok zseniálisak és melyek csak a történelem véletlenei.

items.explanation: F – Losing answers before we find them (elveszítjük a válaszokat, mielőtt megtalálnánk őket). A legtöbb fajt még le sem írták, és sok kihal, mielőtt bárki megvizsgálhatná – vagyis olyan megoldások vesznek el, amelyeket még nem ismerünk (mint egy könyvtár, amelyet azelőtt égetnek el, hogy bárki elolvasta volna a könyveit).
items.evidence: every time a species dies out, we also lose solutions that took millions of years to develop

wrongOptions.E: Az E a 0. bekezdés (példa) címe: ott a természet évmilliárdos „előnyéről” van szó; itt viszont a fajok kihalása és a megoldások elvesztése a fő gondolat.
